title: Find Pattern in Infinite Stream II
statement:
This is an interactive problem. Bits (`0` or `1`) arrive from a stream that never ends; its positions are numbered from `0`. You only reach it through the object `infiniteStream`, whose one method `infiniteStream.next()` hands back the bit at the next unread position (position `0` first, then `1`, and so on); bits cannot be read twice. You also get a binary array `pattern`.

Return the first position `i` at which the stream contains `pattern` as a contiguous run, that is, the bits at positions `i, i + 1, ..., i + pattern.length - 1` equal `pattern` in order. An occurrence is guaranteed to start among the first 10^5 bits.

Write `findPattern(infiniteStream, pattern)`. A case is stored as `[stream, pattern]`, where `stream` is a finite block of bits that the judge repeats forever (`[0, 1, 1]` means `0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, ...`) to build `infiniteStream`. Your code never sees that block, and a run that calls `next` more than 110,000 times is stopped.
constraints: pattern starts within the first 10^5 bits of the stream
In a case, the repeating block has 1 to 2000 bits
api: findPattern(infiniteStream: InfiniteStream, pattern: number[]): number, with interface InfiniteStream { next(): number }
notes:
## Intuition

The stream is read once, left to right, so after every new bit we must know whether the pattern has just been completed. Keeping all bits and comparing the last `m` of them with `pattern` costs O(m) per bit, which is too slow when the pattern has 10^4 bits and the match starts near position 10^5. Knuth–Morris–Pratt keeps one number instead: `matched`, how many leading bits of `pattern` the stream currently ends with. When the next bit breaks that match, a table built from the pattern alone says the longest shorter prefix that the stream still ends with, so no bit is ever re-read.

## Approach

1. Build `fail`: `fail[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `pattern[0..i]` that is also its suffix. Grow `border` while bits agree and fall back through `fail` when they do not.
2. Read bits one by one; `position` is the index of the bit just read.
3. While `bit` cannot extend the current match, set `matched = fail[matched - 1]`.
4. If `bit` equals `pattern[matched]`, increase `matched`.
5. Once `matched === m`, the pattern ends at `position`; return `position - m + 1`.

## Example 1, step by step

`pattern = [0, 1]`, so `fail = [0, 0]`. The stream begins `1, 1, 1, 0, 1`. Positions 0, 1 and 2 bring a `1`, which is not `pattern[0]`, so `matched` stays `0`. Position 3 brings `0`, so `matched = 1`. Position 4 brings `1 = pattern[1]`, so `matched = 2 = m`, and the answer is `4 - 2 + 1 = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m + s), where s is the number of bits read (the answer plus m): `matched` rises by at most one per bit, and each fallback lowers it.
- Space: O(m) for `fail`; the stream itself is never stored.

## Pitfalls

- Resetting `matched` to 0 on a mismatch misses overlapping matches: with pattern `[1, 1, 0, 1]` and stream `1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1`, the match starts at 2 inside an earlier partial match.
- Use a `while` for the fallback, not an `if`: one step back may still not fit the new bit.
- Return the start of the match, not the position of its last bit.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `m` | length of `pattern` |
| `fail` | longest proper border length of each pattern prefix |
| `border` | current border length while building `fail` |
| `matched` | how many leading pattern bits the stream currently ends with |
| `position` | index of the bit just read |
| `bit` | the bit just read |
